name: change-of-control
description: Extract change-of-control provisions from a contract. Designed against Harvey LAB's `extract-change-of-control-provisions` rubric (55 criteria, 8-contract corpus). Per-column field design forces specific assertions the rubric demands (section numbers, exact quotes, risk ratings, cross-references) that free-form prose typically scatters across paragraphs.

columns.description: Act as a corporate associate identifying the target's counterparty in this contract. Look at the preamble or signature block. Return the counterparty's exact legal name (the entity that is NOT the target / acquiring company).

Classify the contract's primary type. Use 'master_services_agreement' (MSA) for ongoing service contracts; 'supply_agreement' for goods supply contracts; 'license' for IP/technology licenses; 'employment' for individual employment agreements (not service contracts). When ambiguous, prefer the document's own self-label in the title.
Look in the 'Governing Law' section. Return the named jurisdiction (e.g., 'Delaware', 'New York', 'California'). Do NOT include the venue/forum clause if separate. If unstated, omit.

Section number where the contract DEFINES 'Change of Control' (e.g., 'Section 1.01', '§ 1.1(c)'). Look in the Definitions section first. If the contract has no separate change-of-control definition (relies on assignment-clause language only), return 'NONE — no separate definition'.

Verbatim text of the change-of-control definition clause. Include the exact ownership/voting threshold, what counts as a triggering event (merger, consolidation, sale, etc.), and any 'direct or indirect' qualifying language. If no separate definition exists, return the substantive equivalent from the assignment clause.

True if the change-of-control definition explicitly includes 'indirect' changes of ownership or control (e.g., 'any direct or indirect change in the ultimate ownership'). The presence of 'indirect' creates broader risk because parent-level transactions can trigger. False if only direct changes are covered.

Section number containing the anti-assignment / consent-to-assignment clause (e.g., 'Section 14.2', '§ 22.1'). This may be DIFFERENT from the change-of-control definition section. Some contracts (commodity supply, MSAs) have only an anti-assignment clause and no separate change-of-control definition.

Verbatim text of the anti-assignment clause. CRITICAL: include any 'whether by operation of law or otherwise' phrasing — this language is the test for whether reverse-triangular mergers trigger the clause. Also capture the consent standard if embedded ('not to be unreasonably withheld', 'in the sole discretion of', etc.).

True if the anti-assignment clause explicitly includes 'operation of law' or equivalent. This is the key legal test: under a reverse-triangular merger (where the target survives), 'operation of law' phrasing triggers the clause; absence of such phrasing typically does NOT trigger. False if the clause only covers voluntary/direct assignments.

True if the contract requires the counterparty's consent before a change of control / assignment closes. False otherwise. This determines whether Apex needs to negotiate consent before signing the merger.
Section number granting / requiring consent (e.g., 'Section 22.1'). May be the same as anti_assignment_section.

The standard for granting / withholding consent. 'reasonableness' = 'not to be unreasonably withheld'. 'absolute_discretion' = 'in the sole and absolute discretion of'. 'objective_standards' = consent tied to specified financial / operational metrics. 'unspecified' = the section requires consent but does not state a standard.

True if a change of control gives the counterparty the right to terminate the contract. False otherwise. This is distinct from triggers_consent — some contracts allow assignment with consent but ALSO allow termination if consent is withheld.
Section number granting the termination right on change of control (e.g., 'Section 9.1', 'Section 22.4'). If termination is conditional on consent being withheld, name the section that conditions it.
Number of days' notice required before termination becomes effective. E.g., '120 days' notice' → 120. If termination is immediate, return 0. If unstated, omit.

Days the target has to cure a triggered termination. E.g., '30-day cure period' → 30. CRITICAL: a no-cure-period clause (cure_period_days=0) is significantly higher risk than a 30+ day cure. If unstated, omit.

Dollar amount of any early-termination fee triggered on change-of-control termination. E.g., a $3,240,000 lease early-termination fee. Return as money (amount + currency). If no termination fee, omit.

Verbatim text of any buyout / forced-sale formula triggered on change of control. E.g., '4.5x trailing twelve-month EBITDA' from a JV agreement. Capture the multiple, the base metric (EBITDA / revenue / book value), and the trailing-period definition. Forced-buyout provisions often represent the largest financial exposure in a deal.

The annual revenue exposure if this contract is lost (terminated, not renewed) post-closing. Look for the contract's revenue contribution in disclosure schedules, supplier-of-record reports, or stated dollar amounts in the contract itself. E.g., '$36.2 million in trailing twelve-month revenue' for the Northland MSA. CRITICAL for risk-rating concentration analysis — the target's largest customer / supplier exposures drive the deal-killer risks.

Percentage of the target's total revenue that this contract represents. E.g., '19.3' for a contract producing 19.3% of total revenue. If only a dollar exposure is stated and total revenue is computable from elsewhere in the corpus, do that calculation. If neither is computable, omit. Concentration > 10% generally elevates risk.

For employment / equity contracts: dollar value of equity that accelerates on change of control. E.g., '$967,230' from an executive's RSU acceleration on a single-trigger CoC clause. Capture the methodology if visible (units * VWAP, etc.). Omit for non-employment contracts.

For employment / equity contracts: True if equity vesting accelerates SOLELY on the change-of-control event (single-trigger). False if the acceleration also requires a qualifying termination after CoC (double-trigger). Single-trigger is significantly higher risk because it forces value transfer regardless of post-closing intentions.

List of THIRD-PARTY systems, software, or services that this contract depends on or references but are NOT themselves under review as separate contracts. E.g., a Hendricks License Agreement that embeds the FlowLogic algorithm in the AX-7000 product line — return ['FlowLogic algorithm', 'AX-7000 product line']. A JV agreement mentioning 'Crestline ERP Platform' as a critical IT system → return ['Crestline ERP Platform']. CRITICAL: this column surfaces cross-document dependencies that downstream cross-reference checks will flag as separate review items.

List of OTHER contracts referenced by this one (e.g., 'Master Services Agreement dated 2019-04-12' or 'Schedule 3.07 of the Credit Agreement'). Each entry is a contract identifier or short description. Used by cross-document KG queries to find dependency chains and conflicting provisions.

Apply the legal test: under a reverse-triangular merger (Merger Sub merges into target, target survives as wholly-owned subsidiary of Acquirer), does this contract's anti-assignment / change-of-control clause TRIGGER? Decision rules: (1) If the contract has 'operation of law or otherwise' phrasing AND the contract is a sales-of-goods MSA, cite UCC § 2-210 and conclude 'jurisdiction-dependent — likely TRIGGERS in many states'. (2) If the contract has explicit 'change of control' definition with ownership-threshold language, conclude 'TRIGGERS regardless of merger structure'. (3) If only voluntary-assignment language without 'operation of law', conclude 'likely DOES NOT TRIGGER under reverse-triangular structure'. Return a short paragraph applying these rules to THIS contract's clause.

Assign one of four risk ratings to this contract. CRITICAL = deal-killer or > $25M exposure, no-cure single-trigger, mandatory consent the counterparty can withhold absolutely. HIGH = significant financial exposure (> $5M) OR a hard termination right with limited cure. MEDIUM = consent required but with reasonableness standard, < $5M exposure. LOW = no CoC trigger, only consent for assignment of specific rights, immaterial exposure. Default to the HIGHER rating when uncertain — undisclosed risks are far more costly than over-flagging.

One- or two-sentence justification for the risk_rating. Cite the specific clause sections + dollar exposures that drove the rating. E.g., 'CRITICAL — single-trigger termination on 30-day notice (Section 9.1) plus $52.3M revenue exposure (FlowLogic embedded in AX-7000 product line).'

Pre-closing or post-closing action items required. E.g., ['Obtain landlord consent under Section 22.1 prior to closing', 'Negotiate waiver of single-trigger acceleration', 'Confirm UCC § 2-210 jurisdictional analysis']. Each item is a specific imperative naming the section / clause / counterparty involved. These items feed the closing-checklist deliverable downstream.

metadata.produces: per-contract structured record + cross-contract risk roll-up via downstream graph queries

notes:
Schema field design notes:

- The 28 columns map to Harvey's 55 criteria as roughly 1-to-2 (one column → 1-2 specific rubric items). The richness comes from forcing the LLM to fill SPECIFIC fields rather than write free-form prose.
- Sections are split into definition_section + assignment_section + consent_section + termination_section because contracts often reference all four for the same triggering event. Free-form prose collapses these into 'the change-of-control provision' and loses the specificity rubrics demand.
- `dependent_systems` and `cross_referenced_contracts` are the cross-reference fields. Downstream kaos-graph queries find systems that appear here but aren't themselves under review (catches Crestline-ERP class failures).
- `reverse_triangular_analysis` is required (not optional) — forcing this analysis on every contract closes the cross-cutting gap that free-form Sonnet missed.
- `risk_rating` is required + enum-constrained. Solves Harvey's risk-rating completeness criteria (C-048: rate every contract).
- `revenue_concentration_pct` may need calculation post-extraction (e.g., revenue_exposure / total_revenue across the corpus). Downstream code can compute this from extracted cells.

Calibration: Harvey's published recall floors for analogous schemas are 96.49% (court-opinion) to 99.66% (merger-agreement). 95% is the conservative initial floor for a 28-column M&A-review schema; will be re-calibrated after live runs.
